The LC-3 is a small 16-bit instructional architecture: eight general-purpose registers, a program counter, condition flags, and a 2^{16}-word address space. At each step the machine fetches a word from memory at the PC, decodes it as one of fourteen opcodes (from arithmetic and bitwise operations to loads, stores, branches, jumps, and subroutine calls), then updates registers, memory, and control flow accordingly. Beyond those opcodes, LC-3 programs rely on trap routines for console I/O and on memory-mapped I/O for the keyboard—so a faithful simulator must implement both the core instructions and this I/O story. For more on the architecture, see here.

The code in LC3-Lean is laid out as follows:
register and flag state lives in LC3Lean/Registers.lean,
the flat memory model in LC3Lean/Memory.lean,
opcode decoding in LC3Lean/Instructions.lean,
the fetch–decode–execute step and per-opcode semantics in LC3Lean/Execution.lean,
The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean. If you open those modules, every informal claim in this paragraph—word size, register count, opcode coverage, traps, MMIO—is meant to be visible as definitions and executable code rather than hand-waving.
The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean.
For full details, see this page.

"Formally verified" here means that Lean checks mathematical theorems relating the implementation above to an explicit ISA-level specification of how each instruction may read and write registers and memory. Those theorems are stated and proved in the LC3Correct package—especially LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean, with supporting lemmas about registers and memory in LC3Correct/RegisterLemmas.lean and LC3Correct/MemoryLemmas.lean. Together they aim to capture, opcode by opcode, that the Lean executor’s effect on machine state matches the spec encoded alongside it. All proofs pass without sorry!

The boundary worth keeping in mind is the thin C shim (c/terminal.c) used for POSIX terminal raw mode and polling: it affects how characters reach your screen and keyboard, but the LC-3 machine semantics and the correctness proofs live on the Lean side. Readers who want the precise logical statement for a single opcode should start from LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean and follow the definitions it references—the prose here is only a map to those lemmas.
For full details, see this page.
During Q1 of 2026 we worked building out CompPoly, a formally verified model of computable polynomials in Lean. The purpose of CompPoly is to provide a computable base for the specs in Arklib.

My thoughts on computable specifications are still developing. They are growing out of an interest during my PhD in the integrity of formal specifications in the case of smart contracts. zkVMs and SNARKS also have complicated specifications, but for a different reason than smart contracts. Whereas smart contract specifications have difficult-to-define, high-level, socio-economic properties that one must aim at with a spec, the specs of zkVMs are complex because they correspond to some pretty intense mathematics. Just stating the desired properties requires quite a bit of machinery -- see Arklib for a taste of that.

So, we can write complex mathematical specifications in Lean - great, what does computability add to this, or any specification? For one, it lets you run tests. Having tests lets you test the integrity of your spec and test it in sort of a meta- way. It helps build confidence that the spec was built out correctly, something that is difficult (impossible?) to really know.

I have written before about metaspecifications, or formal specifications of specifications, in the context of smart contracts. I really believe that metaspecifications can add a lot to the security of smart contracts, but a lot of theory has to be built up (even just developed from a cryptoeconomic point of view) before this becomes a reasonable strategy for contracts in the wild.

However, metaspecifications already show up in cryptography! An implementation has a specification, the design of the cryptographic system or protocol (e.g. FRI). The system or protocol is defined in mathematical terms, with assumptions, and with associated proofs of security. Security proofs (reduction proofs) show that if the cryptographic protocol fails, then some assumption of the system was violated. This is a metaspecification!

But, as with all specifications, it is very hard to be sure that your specification is correct. This is where computability comes in. Having an executable/computable specification means that you can run tests on it, further extending your specification in an informal way. It makes your spec act more like software, and in some sense makes it stronger as a specification because as a program that runs it is closer to the thing that you're verifying.

Lean is of course a great place for this. It is easy to go between computable and non-computable terms, spec and implementation, and more and more of the infrastructure of verification is becoming available in Lean.

fr:title.text: Smart Contract Design, Specification, and Verification

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Smart Contract Design, Specification, and Verification

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Smart contracts are interesting from the perspective of formal specification and verification because:

html:ol.html:li: they are typically small in size, with a deterministic and well-defined execution environment, making them feasible to formally reason about in a short time frame, and
they often manage huge sums of money (so the incentives line up).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Furthermore, because smart contracts act as social and financial intermediaries, they often have extremely interesting (and nontrivia) specifications, which warrants a study not only of the science of going from specification to verification (formal proof), but of the specifications themselves as independent, mathematical objects.

Speaking more broadly, formal verification in proof assistants is interesting because in the robustly mathematical setting provided by proof assistants, one can state and prove arbitrary properties.
This may be a blessing and a curse. Much like with programming languages, being able to state and do arbitrary things is not always an advantage.
Due to the extreme flexibility, formal counterparts of informal specifications can vary widely without an obvious way to compare them or evaluate them for correctness or practical utility (for more on this see the introduction to my PhD thesis).

In my PhD and my subsequent writing (e.g. this paper or my research statement), I have argued that the robustly mathematical setting of proof assistants offers us an opportunity for unmatched rigor, but we must draw on mathematical practice and tradition and use them in a more sophisticated way than we are using them now. There is much to be learned from the ongoing work in the formalization of mathematics and formal specification and verification in proof assistants more broadly, from theoretical and practical perspectives.

I am also interested more broadly in type theory and formal proof, especially as they relate to proof assistants. This has included some preliminary work in HoTT on the formal side, but ongoing work in the formalization of mathematics in Lean is deeply interesting to me as a peripheral development to my work.

A systematic study of the cryptography and machine architecture that zkVMs and SNARKs are built from, topic by topic. It is the theory behind the snarkification work: ArkLib, CompPoly, and Clean formalise these protocols in Lean, and formalisation rewards local knowledge — a folding lemma can be proved without holding the whole argument in view. The purpose of a corpus like this one is to hold the whole argument.

The spine is the pipeline every modern proof system follows. A computation becomes a constraint system; the constraint system becomes an interactive oracle proof; the oracles are realised by commitments; the interaction is removed by Fiat–Shamir; the result is made recursive and wrapped around a virtual machine. Each section below is one stage of that pipeline, which is also roughly how ArkLib is organised — so a page here usually has a Lean file behind it.

Every leaf has the same shape: what the page covers, the questions it should answer, and where to read. A page is complete when its subject can be reconstructed from it without the sources — for a protocol, that means the theorem stated with its assumptions, and what breaks when one of them is dropped.

How a computation becomes algebra. Three formats dominate — R1CS, Plonkish, and AIR — and CCS is the claim that they are one object with different sparsity patterns.

Clean sits at this layer: an embedded DSL that writes circuits for these formats in Lean, with the specification and the soundness proof next to the circuit. The open question is what "this circuit implements this specification" should mean, and which arithmetisation makes that statement easiest to prove — the same question as for smart contract specifications, with better-behaved mathematics.
The oldest of the three formats and still the one the folding literature is written in.

Questions this page should answer:
The format: (Az) \circ (Bz) = Cz, the instance and witness split, and what "satisfying" means.
Sparsity, and why the prover's cost is an MSM or a sparse-polynomial commitment rather than an FFT.
Relaxed and committed R1CS, the variants folding needs.
The cost of a range check or a bit decomposition here, compared with a lookup in a Plonkish system.
zkLean as the R1CS-facing circuit DSL in the verified-zkEVM effort.
Gate constraints plus a wiring argument, with lookups bolted on. "Plonkish" is used loosely across implementations, so the term needs a precise statement of what it covers.

Questions this page should answer:
Gate constraints and selectors; custom gates and what raising the degree costs.
Copy constraints via a permutation argument — the mechanism that distinguishes Plonkish from AIR.
Lookup tables in the halo2 sense: regions, fixed columns, and the developer-facing cost model.
Preprocessing: what is fixed at setup and what varies per instance.
Where Plonkish and AIR genuinely differ, once cross-table lookups are available to both.
The arithmetisation the STARK toolkits consume, and the entry point for the formalisation work: Plonky3 and Stwo both take an AIR as input, and Clean targets it.

Questions this page should answer:
Execution trace, transition constraints, boundary constraints; the uniformity assumption that makes the format succinct.
Constraint degree, and how it propagates into the quotient polynomial and the rate.
Preprocessed columns and randomised AIR with preprocessing (RAP) — what the extra randomness is for.
Multiple tables and cross-table constraints; how a zkVM's chips are expressed.
Padding, and the soundness bugs that live in the boundary between padded and real rows.

Customisable constraint systems, proposed as the generalisation that has R1CS, Plonkish, and AIR as instances. Worth understanding both as a claim about expressiveness and as the format HyperNova folds.

Questions this page should answer:
The definition, and the explicit embeddings of the three formats into it.
What the unification buys: one folding scheme, one commitment interface, one soundness proof.
What it costs — where a CCS encoding is asymptotically or concretely worse than the native format.
Whether the same unification is the right structuring principle for a formal library, or whether ArkLib's per-system files are better.

Modern zkVMs are mostly lookups: instruction semantics, range checks, bitwise operations, and memory consistency all become table queries. This is where the prover's time goes, so it is where the interesting engineering is.

Questions this page should answer:
The logarithmic-derivative identity (logUp) and why it replaced grand-product multiset checks.
logUp-GKR: applying sumcheck to the fraction identity to avoid committing to O(m) field elements.
Lasso: the lookup relation as a = M \cdot T with M sparse, and decomposability for tables of size 2^{64} and beyond.
logup* and the small-table indexed case.
The "lookup singularity" claim from 2023 — how much of it held, measured in real zkVM benchmarks.
What a lookup argument's soundness proof actually requires, and what the Jolt semantics verification found.
Sources: The logUp-GKR protocol, Introducing Lasso and Jolt, logup*, Verifying Jolt zkVM Lookup Semantics.
The arguments that enforce global consistency across a trace, as opposed to row-local constraints. Memory is the hard case and the usual source of unsoundness.

Questions this page should answer:
Permutation and multiset-equality arguments; the grand product and its logUp replacement.
Offline memory checking: reads and writes as multisets of (address, value, timestamp) tuples, and the conditions that make it sound.
Address-sorted versus timestamp-sorted formulations, and what each costs.
Read-write memory in the folding setting.
The constraint that is always forgotten: monotonicity of timestamps, and what a missing range check on it permits.
Sources: Nebula: efficient read-write memory, ArkLib's ProofSystem/ConstraintSystem/MemoryChecking.lean.

fr:title.text: Clean: Circuits and Their Specifications in Lean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Clean: Circuits and Their Specifications in Lean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An embedded Lean DSL for writing zk circuits against AIR, Plonkish, and R1CS, built by zkSecurity under a verified-zkEVM grant. Circuit, specification, and proof live in the same file — an arrangement smart contract verification has never had.

Questions this page should answer:
How a circuit is represented, and what the proof obligation looks like — the precise form of "this circuit is sound with respect to this specification".
Completeness as a separate obligation, and whether it is discharged or assumed.
Lookups and VM-like table ensembles: the recent generalisation, and what it makes provable end to end.
Witness generation by compilation to an intermediate representation, and whether the generator is verified against the constraints.
Backends — plonky3 now, stwo and R1CS variants planned — and what a backend has to guarantee.
How Clean's circuit specs should meet ArkLib's protocol specs. It is the load-bearing seam between the two libraries.
Sources: clean, Introducing clean.

The component that turns an oracle in an IOP into something a real verifier can query. Swapping the commitment scheme changes a system's proof size, its trust assumptions, and its post-quantum status while leaving the arithmetisation untouched — which is why this is the layer where systems are usually differentiated.
ArkLib splits these into ordinary and functional commitments; understanding why that split is the right one is part of the point of these pages.
What a polynomial commitment scheme has to provide, stated precisely enough that a protocol can be proved secure against the interface rather than against a particular scheme.

Questions this page should answer:
Syntax: setup, commit, open, verify — and which parameters are public.
Binding, evaluation binding, and extractability; which one a BCS-style compilation actually needs.
Batch openings and homomorphism, and how much of a protocol's efficiency depends on them.
Functional commitments as the generalisation, and why ArkLib separates Commitments/Functional from Commitments/Ordinary.
Multilinear versus univariate interfaces, and the adapters between them.
The commitment underneath every hash-based system. Simple enough that it is easy to skip and consequential enough that the hash choice dominates prover time.

Questions this page should answer:
Position binding, and what a Merkle commitment does not give you.
Batched openings and path deduplication; where proof size actually goes.
Salting and its role in zero knowledge — and in ArkLib's Salt.lean.
Hash cost as the prover's real bottleneck; arity and tree shape tradeoffs.
The formalisation: what ArkLib's Merkle tree development proves, and what it assumes about the hash.
Constant-size proofs and a constant-time verifier, at the price of a trusted setup and a pairing-friendly curve. Still the endpoint of most wrapping pipelines because the on-chain verifier is cheap.

Questions this page should answer:
The scheme and its security assumption; what the structured reference string contains.
The pairing check, and why the verifier is constant-time regardless of degree.
Batching and multi-point openings.
Trusted setup in practice: ceremonies, updatability, and what a compromised setup permits.
Why it does not scale to zkVM-sized traces, and where it survives anyway.
Logarithmic-size proofs without a trusted setup, over ordinary elliptic curve groups. Largely displaced by hash-based schemes in the zkVM setting, so the useful question is where it still wins.

Questions this page should answer:
The Bulletproofs-style recursive halving argument and its transcript.
Proof size against verifier time: the linear verifier is the catch.
Accumulation and the Halo line, as the precursor to modern folding.
Discrete-log security, and the post-quantum consequence.
The tensor-commitment lineage: commit to a matrix whose rows are codewords, and test proximity by sampling columns. Basefold is where this line and the FRI line merge.

Questions this page should answer:
The tensor structure and the proximity test; why the verifier's work is O(\sqrt {n}) in the plain construction.
Brakedown's linear-time encodable codes, and the tradeoff against proof size.
Basefold: foldable codes plus sumcheck, giving a multilinear commitment from a code that need not be Reed–Solomon.
Which codes are admissible, and what the soundness proof needs from them.
How this family compares with WHIR on verifier cost and on argument size.
Sources: SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments and Low-Degree Tests.
Committing to values that live in a tiny field without paying extension-field prices for every one of them. The problem Binius exists to solve, and the reason ArkLib has a RingSwitching directory.

Questions this page should answer:
Why a naive commitment to \mathbb {F}_2 values wastes almost all of its capacity, and what packing recovers.
The ring-switching reduction: a claim over the extension becomes a claim over the base, or the reverse.
Where soundness needs the large field regardless, and how much of the argument can stay small.
The interaction with binary towers specifically, versus 31-bit primes.
What ArkLib formalises here and what remains open.
Sources: ArkLib, The Small-Field Turn.

fr:title.text: Low-Degree Testing, from FRI to WHIR

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Low-Degree Testing, from FRI to WHIR

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The heart of the transparent stack. The lineage is short and each step answers one specific complaint: FRI tests proximity to a Reed–Solomon code by folding, STIR attacks its query cost at constant rate, and WHIR attacks STIR's verification cost while joining the univariate and multilinear worlds.

These pages should be the most careful in the corpus. The soundness statements are where the regimes matter, where the deployed parameters are conjectural, and where ArkLib's hardest formalisation work sits.
Fast Reed–Solomon Interactive Oracle Proof of Proximity. The protocol most of the deployed proving stack rests on, and the one every construction later in this section is a response to.

Questions this page should answer:
The folding map: halving the degree by splitting into even and odd parts and taking a random combination. Why the folded word is a codeword when the original is.
Commit phase and query phase; the round-consistency check the verifier performs.
Parameters and their interaction: rate, folding factor, number of rounds, number of query repetitions.
Prover cost — encoding, Merkle hashing, and where the time actually goes.
The soundness statement, with the regime named explicitly.
What ArkLib's ProofSystem/Fri states, and how far the proof gets.
Reading: Ben-Sasson, Bentov, Horesh, and Riabzev, Fast Reed–Solomon Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (ICALP 2018); the SoK for the corrected attributions.

fr:title.text: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same protocol has different soundness depending on how far from the code you are willing to reason, and the parameters used in production sit in the regime where the analysis is conjectural. This page is the reason list decoding is in this corpus at all.

Questions this page should answer:
Unique decoding, the Johnson bound, and capacity: the guarantee each yields and the parameters each licenses.
What must be conjectured to reach capacity, and the precise statement of each conjecture.
Threshold halving, and what it establishes above the Johnson bound.
The accounting from soundness error to bits of security, including grinding.
Which deployed systems set parameters in which regime — and whether the choice is documented anywhere citable.
Sources: SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments, On Reed–Solomon Proximity Gaps Conjectures, FRI Soundness Above the Johnson Bound.

Sampling outside the evaluation domain, which appears in deployed provers for reasons that are not the reason usually given. The SoK's claim that the deployed trick and the low-degree-test modification are routinely conflated needs to be nailed down here.

Questions this page should answer:
DEEP quotienting: what the quotient is, and what an out-of-domain evaluation buys the analysis.
The conjecture on classical list-decodability that DEEP-FRI introduced.
The two distinct uses — constraint batching in a STARK versus the low-degree test itself — and which one production code implements.
Where the extension field is forced (the out-of-domain point lives there), and the cost.
Sources: SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments.
Two engineering devices that materially change the security accounting, and are therefore easy to get wrong.

Questions this page should answer:
Batched FRI: many words, one folding argument. What the random combination costs in soundness, and what ArkLib's BatchedFri states.
Batching across constraint polynomials in a STARK, and how it interacts with DEEP.
Proof-of-work grinding: converting prover hash work into verifier confidence, and the exact form of the resulting bound.
How many bits of a deployed security level come from grinding rather than from the protocol.
Whether grinding is accounted for in the round-by-round analysis or bolted on afterwards.
Shift To Improve Rate. FRI keeps the rate fixed across rounds and pays for it in queries; STIR improves the rate each round instead.

Questions this page should answer:
The rate-shifting step, and why it reduces query complexity rather than prover time.
The query complexity comparison with FRI, stated with the constants.
What it costs: verifier work, argument size, and round count.
The soundness analysis and which regime it lands in.
ArkLib's ProofSystem/Stir: the formal statement and its current status.
Sources: Arnon, Chiesa, Fenzi, and Yogev, STIR; ArkLib.
The current endpoint of the lineage: a multilinear commitment with a very fast verifier, unifying the Reed–Solomon proximity line with the tensor-commitment line that Basefold began.

Questions this page should answer:
The construction, and where sumcheck enters the low-degree test.
How a multilinear claim is served by a univariate proximity test — the translation, and its cost.
The verifier-time claim, and what it is measured against.
Which of STIR's ideas it keeps and which it discards.
ArkLib's WHIR formalisation: what is proved, and what the remaining obligations are.
Sources: Arnon, Chiesa, Fenzi, and Yogev, WHIR; SoK: Hash-Based Polynomial Commitments; ArkLib.

Named systems, each a particular choice of arithmetisation, commitment, and field. Once the layers below are understood these should be readable as combinations rather than as separate inventions — and where a system is not just a combination, that is the interesting part.
Three group elements, a circuit-specific trusted setup, and a verifier cheap enough for the EVM. Obsolete as a zkVM backend and unavoidable as a wrapper.

Questions this page should answer:
QAPs: from R1CS to a divisibility claim.
The proof and the verification equation; why it is exactly three elements.
The security argument in the algebraic group model, and what AGM assumes about the adversary. ArkLib has an AGM directory for this.
Circuit-specific setup as the practical objection, and what universal setup changed.
The system that made Plonkish a category, and the implementation that most auditors' intuitions were formed on.

Questions this page should answer:
The protocol: gate identity, permutation argument, quotient, and opening.
Universal and updatable setup, and what it removed as an operational problem.
Halo2's departures: the table and region model, and the commitment swap from KZG to IPA in some deployments.
Where the lookup argument entered, and how it changed circuit design practice.
ArkLib's ProofSystem/Plonk and ConstraintSystem/Plonk.lean: which layer each covers.

R1CS proved with sumcheck instead of quotients, which removes the FFT and moves the cost into a sparse polynomial commitment. It is also one of the systems ArkLib has formalised, so it is a good place to read a full argument in Lean.

Questions this page should answer:
The reduction from R1CS satisfiability to a sumcheck claim.
Sparse polynomial commitment (Spark) and why the matrices' sparsity is what makes this cheap.
Prover cost profile against a Plonkish system on the same circuit.
The line from here to HyperNova, which folds the same shape of claim.

Plonkish constraints over the Boolean hypercube rather than a multiplicative subgroup, so the prover never runs an FFT. The clearest statement of what moving to multilinear representations does and does not buy.

Questions this page should answer:
The translation of gate and wiring constraints into sumcheck claims.
What replaces the quotient polynomial and the low-degree test.
Cost profile: no FFT, more commitment work, different memory behaviour.
High-degree custom gates, which this handles better than univariate Plonk.
Why the field choice matters less here than in the FRI world — or whether it does.

fr:title.text: STARKs: Plonky3, Stwo, and Circle STARKs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: STARKs: Plonky3, Stwo, and Circle STARKs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AIR plus FRI, over a small field, as a reusable toolkit rather than a single protocol. This is the layer the Rust-to-Lean extraction work targets: Plonky3 in Lean, with proofs about what it computes.

Questions this page should answer:
The STARK protocol end to end: trace, constraints, quotient, commitment, low-degree test.
Plonky3 as a toolkit — what is configurable (field, hash, PCS, folding factor) and what is fixed.
Stwo and the circle domain: Mersenne31 has no large smooth subgroup, so what replaces it and what changes in the constraint system.
Circle STARKs' vanishing polynomials and the extra care their boundary constraints need.
Where the two toolkits agree, since both consume an AIR — and what that means for Clean targeting both.
Sources: Plonky3, stwo, Buterin, Exploring circle STARKs.

A proof system built from the ground up on binary tower fields, with ring switching as the mechanism that keeps small values cheap. The most complete demonstration of the small-field argument taken to its limit.

Questions this page should answer:
The stack: tower fields, multilinear polynomials, a small-field commitment, and sumcheck-based constraint checking.
How a bit-level computation avoids paying for embedding into a large field.
Flock, which specialises the same idea to large batches of one Boolean circuit and is what made conventional hashes cheap enough to prove that Ethereum dropped Poseidon.
Where the extension field is still required, and what fraction of the work it accounts for.
The measured comparison against 31-bit prime systems, and on which workloads it holds.
ArkLib's ProofSystem/Binius and RingSwitching: what is stated and what is proved.
Sources: Binary tower fields, SNARKs on binary fields, ArkLib.

How a proof about a long computation is assembled from proofs about short ones. Every zkVM that proves a real workload is doing this, and it is where the soundness argument becomes hardest to keep track of — the Nova bug is the standing example.
The definitions that folding and recursion are trying to achieve, and the overhead problem that shapes every construction: the verifier has to be expressible as a circuit in the system it verifies.

Questions this page should answer:
Incrementally verifiable computation and proof-carrying data: the statements, and the knowledge soundness they require.
Recursion overhead: what a verifier-in-circuit costs, and which components dominate (hashing, MSM, field arithmetic).
Cycles of curves, and why hash-based systems avoid the problem differently.
How the security loss compounds over recursion depth.

Folding two R1CS instances into one without proving either, deferring all the SNARK work to the end. Also a case study in why this material needs formalising: a soundness bug was found in the published scheme.

Questions this page should answer:
Relaxed R1CS and committed relaxed R1CS: why the relaxation is needed to make folding close.
The folding step and its knowledge-soundness argument.
Why the recursive circuit is small — the folding verifier, not a SNARK verifier.
The bug: what the flaw was, what it permitted, and which part of the argument would have caught it under machine-checked scrutiny.
Sources: how Nova got broken, awesome-folding.
The folding design space after Nova: which constraint systems can be folded, how many instances at once, and what the recursive circuit costs.

Questions this page should answer:
HyperNova: folding CCS, with per-step cost dominated by one MSM.
ProtoStar: folding arbitrary low-degree polynomial maps, and what that generality buys.
ProtoGalaxy and multi-instance folding; KiloNova and non-uniform PCD.
The axes to compare on: constraint system, instances per fold, recursive circuit size, assumptions.
Which of these is the right target for a formalisation, given that the definitions are still moving.
Sources: HyperNova, multi-instance folding techniques, awesome-folding.
Splitting a long execution into segments that can be proved independently and in parallel. The mechanism that makes zkVM proving a distributed job rather than a single machine's problem.

Questions this page should answer:
Segmenting a trace: what state must be carried across a boundary, and how it is committed.
The consistency argument between shards, especially for memory.
Aggregating shard proofs into one, and the recursion tree's shape.
How SP1 and RISC Zero each do it, and what their differences imply.
The soundness surface this adds — a shard boundary is a place to forget a constraint.
The last step of a deployed pipeline: convert a large STARK proof into something an on-chain verifier can check cheaply, usually by proving the STARK verifier inside a pairing-based system.

Questions this page should answer:
The wrapping chain in a real system, layer by layer, with proof sizes at each step.
Arithmetising a hash-based verifier: which parts are expensive and why.
Gas cost of the final verifier, and what it constrains upstream.
The trust and assumption stack the wrap introduces — a trusted setup at the end of a transparent pipeline.
Whether the composed security is stated anywhere precisely enough to formalise.

Everything above, wrapped around an instruction set so that a program rather than a circuit is the thing being proved. A zkVM decomposes into three layers — the ISA, the VM architecture, and the proving layer — and most design disagreements are about where to put work between them.

This is the object the verified zkEVM effort is ultimately aimed at. A machine semantics in Lean is the first half of the statement one wants to prove about a zkVM; LC3 in Lean is that half at small scale.
A map of the layers, so that a claim about one system can be compared with a claim about another. Worth writing before the pages below it.

Questions this page should answer:
The three layers — ISA, VM architecture, proving layer — and the interface between each pair.
What "proving a program" means formally: the relation being proved, and where the program commitment enters.
Which layer a given optimisation belongs to, and which choices are genuinely independent.
The end-to-end statement a zkVM claims, written out in full.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Projects that shaped modern zkVMs.

Whether to prove an existing ISA or design one for provability. RISC-V won the general-purpose end by bringing a compiler toolchain with it; the custom VMs argue the constraint cost is worth the loss.

Questions this page should answer:
RISC-V (RV32I and extensions) as a target: what makes each instruction class expensive to constrain.
Register machines versus stack machines (Miden, zkWasm), and what the memory argument looks like in each.
Purpose-built ISAs — Cairo, Valida — and the specific constraint-cost arguments for them.
Instruction decomposition and the lookup-based approach to semantics that Jolt takes.
The formal ISA specification: what the Sail-to-Lean route gives, and what it does not.
How an execution becomes a set of tables. In practice this is where a zkVM's engineering lives, and the details are what Clean has to be able to express.

Questions this page should answer:
Chips as separate AIRs, one per operation class, connected by cross-table lookups.
The main trace against auxiliary and preprocessed columns; what each costs to commit.
Padding to a power of two, and the constraints that must hold on padded rows.
Witness generation as a first-class cost, and whether the generator is verified against the constraints.
How a single instruction's semantics is spread across chips, and how the pieces are tied back together.

Random-access memory is the hardest part of a zkVM to constrain and the most common source of unsoundness. The general machinery is in permutation and memory arguments; this page is about what the systems actually do.

Questions this page should answer:
Read-write RAM by offline memory checking, as in SP1, Jolt, and RISC Zero.
Paged memory with Merkle verification, which RISC Zero also supports, and when that is preferable.
Stack-based models (Miden, zkWasm) and how their consistency arguments differ.
Memory across shard boundaries — the argument that ties independent segments together.
The concrete cost of a load or store, counted in trace cells and lookups.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, Nebula.

Hand-written circuits for hot operations — hashes, elliptic-curve arithmetic, big-integer work — invoked from the VM instead of being proved instruction by instruction. Large speedups, and a large increase in the amount of hand-written constrained code that has to be correct.

Questions this page should answer:
The mechanism: how a precompile attaches to the trace and how its inputs and outputs are tied to VM state.
The speedups claimed, and on which workloads they decide the benchmark.
The soundness surface: an under-constrained precompile is a complete break, with no compiler to catch it.
Extensibility as a design goal, and what a user-supplied precompile has to prove.
Why this is the most valuable place in the stack to point Clean at.
One entry per system: backend, arithmetisation, field, memory model, and the choice that distinguishes it. The point is a comparison table, not a survey.

Questions this page should answer:
SP1 — RISC-V on Plonky3, precompile-heavy.
Jolt — Lasso-based, lookups for instruction semantics, notably small proofs.
RISC Zero — RISC-V, read-write and paged Merkle memory.
OpenVM — modular and extensible by construction; what its extension interface requires.
Stwo and Cairo — circle STARKs over Mersenne31, with a purpose-built ISA.
Miden and Valida — stack machine and provability-first ISA respectively.
For each: what its soundness rests on that the others' does not.
Sources: SoK: Understanding zkVM, sp1, jolt, risc0, openvm, awesome-zkvm.
What actually costs time, and how to read a published comparison. The target is a cost model good enough to predict the direction of a change before measuring it.

Questions this page should answer:
The cost breakdown: witness generation, hashing, FFTs, MSMs, extension-field arithmetic.
Cycles per second as a metric, and what it hides — precompiles, shard size, security parameters.
Proof size and verifier time across systems, and the recursion that produces the final numbers.
How the field choice shows up in measurements, and why hash rate is often the real headline.
Comparing at equal security: the benchmark question that is usually skipped.
Sources: zkvm-benchmarks.

A catalogue of real failure modes, kept concrete. This page is the evidence for the formalisation work, so it should stay evidence rather than argument. Smart contract vulnerabilities due to poor specification is the same catalogue one domain over, and the failure modes rhyme: code that did what it was specified to do, and a specification that permitted what nobody intended.

Questions this page should answer:
Under-constrained circuits: the general shape, and the canonical examples.
Missing range checks, and why a forgotten monotonicity constraint on memory timestamps is fatal.
Fiat–Shamir misuse: transcripts missing a value, weak domain separation, insufficient challenge space.
Soundness bugs in published schemes rather than implementations — Nova is the example to write up.
Parameter errors: a security level computed in the wrong regime.
Which of these a type system, a linter, an audit, or a proof would each have caught.
Sources: how Nova got broken, How to Prove False Statements.

The reason the rest of this corpus is organised the way it is. The verified zkEVM effort runs three tracks — the zkVM constraints, the EVM semantics, and the cryptography — and ArkLib and CompPoly are the cryptography track.

These pages stay closer to the code than the rest of the corpus, which also makes them the ones most likely to go stale. Related: protocol snarkification, computable specifications, formal verification in proof assistants.
A modular library of formally verified arguments of knowledge in Lean, organised around interactive oracle reductions rather than around individual protocols.

Questions this page should answer:
The directory structure as a design argument: OracleReduction, Commitments, ProofSystem, AGM, and the To* compatibility layers.
What is formalised and to what depth — sumcheck, Spartan, FRI, STIR, WHIR, Binius, Merkle trees, coding theory.
ProofSystem/ConstraintSystem: R1CS, Plonk, lookup, and memory checking in one place.
The security definitions in OracleReduction/Security, which are the real contribution.
What is a statement with no proof yet, and what the roadmap prioritises.
Which developments are blocked on CompPoly.
Sources: ArkLib, ArkLib on lean-lang.org.

Computable polynomials and finite fields in Lean: an executable mirror of the Mathlib definitions, with transfer theorems so proofs can be done on the noncomputable side. The case for computable specifications is made elsewhere; this page is about the artefact.

Questions this page should answer:
The representations chosen, and which operations each makes cheap. See univariate and multilinear polynomials.
The transfer pattern: computable definition, Mathlib definition, proven equivalence, and how proofs move across it.
Field representations and the small fields that matter — see the small-field turn.
What running the spec actually buys: testing a specification against a reference implementation.
Performance in Lean, and whether it is adequate for testing at realistic trace sizes.
Which ArkLib developments depend on it.
Sources: CompPoly.

fr:title.text: VCV-io and Game-Based Cryptography in Lean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: VCV-io and Game-Based Cryptography in Lean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The oracle framework ArkLib is built on: computations with oracle effects, handlers that implement them, and a program logic for the game-hopping arguments that security proofs are written as.

Questions this page should answer:
Oracle computations and simulateQ: implementing a random oracle, logging queries, performing reductions.
The program logic — relational (pRHL-style) and unary modes — and what a game hop looks like as a tactic step.
Primitives already covered: encryption, signatures, sigma protocols, and the Fiat–Shamir and Fischlin transforms.
How ArkLib's adversary model sits on top of this.
What a machine-checked reduction proof costs in effort, compared with the paper proof.
Sources: VCV-io, VCVio: Verified Cryptography in Lean via Oracle Effects and Handlers.
The step that connects a verified protocol to a prover people actually run. Extracting Plonky3 into Lean and proving the extraction agrees with the specification is the current problem.

Questions this page should answer:
hax and its Lean backend: what Rust it accepts, and what it does with the parts it does not.
The functional-equivalence obligation: extracted code against CompPoly-level specifications.
What is assumed rather than proved — unsafe blocks, arithmetic representations, parallelism.
Keeping an extraction current against an upstream repository that moves weekly.
Where proof automation helps, and what the AI-prover pipeline experience report actually reports.
Sources: A Rust-to-Lean Verification Pipeline with AI Provers, Verified-zkEVM overview.

fr:title.text: Specifying the Machine: Sail, LLZK, zkLean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Specifying the Machine: Sail, LLZK, zkLean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The other half of a verified zkVM: a trustworthy specification of the machine being proved, and a way to reason about circuits written in the many DSLs that exist. LC3 in Lean is the same problem at a scale small enough to see all of it.

Questions this page should answer:
The Sail Lean backend: extracting the RISC-V specification into Lean, and what fidelity that gives.
LLZK as an MLIR dialect unifying circuits from different DSLs — what it can and cannot express.
zkLean for R1CS, alongside Clean for AIR.
The gap between an ISA specification and the constraint system claiming to implement it.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The statement at the top of the whole effort, written out honestly: which theorems compose, and which links in the chain are assumptions rather than proofs. Questions this page should answer:
The chain: ISA specification, constraint system, arithmetisation soundness, IOP soundness, commitment security, Fiat–Shamir, recursion, extracted implementation.
Which links are proved today, which are stated, and which are not formalised at all.
The irreducible assumptions: hash security, conjectured proximity bounds, the compiler, the hardware.
Whether "verified" should mean the composed end-to-end theorem, or a set of component theorems with audited seams.
The 2027 target the project set, and what would have to be true for it to be met.
Sources: verified-zkevm.org, Verified-zkEVM overview.

The constraints that come from the deployment target rather than the mathematics. Ethereum wants blocks proved in seconds, on modest hardware, at a security level nobody is willing to negotiate — and increasingly with post-quantum assumptions. fr:title.text: Real-Time Proving and the zkEVM Target

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Real-Time Proving and the zkEVM Target

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What the protocol actually asks of a prover, stated as numbers, and which part of the stack each number constrains.

Questions this page should answer:
The current latency, cost, hardware, and proof-size targets, with a source for each.
Proving an L1 block: what dominates — hashing, signature verification, state access.
Verification on the consumer side: what a home verifier must be able to check, and in what time.
Multi-prover and diversity arguments, and what they assume about implementation independence.
Which targets are met today and which are not.
The hash function is usually the prover's largest single cost, so primitive choice is a proof-system decision rather than an implementation detail.

That framing is what the August 2026 decision to drop Poseidon for L1 inverts, and this page should be written with the reversal in view: hash-friendly SNARKs rather than SNARK-friendly hashes. The cost question below is still the right question — the answer simply stopped selecting for an exotic primitive.

Questions this page should answer:
Arithmetisation-friendly hashes (Poseidon2 and relatives) against standard ones (Keccak, SHA-256, Blake3), counted in constraints.
The security tradeoff: young algebraic designs against well-analysed bit-oriented ones.
Where Ethereum has no choice — Keccak in the state trie, ECDSA in transactions — and what those cost.
Hash rate as a headline benchmark, and what it does and does not predict.
Which hash a Merkle commitment should use at each layer of a recursion.
Hash-based proof systems are plausibly post-quantum and pairing-based ones are not, which turns a cryptographic deadline into an architectural constraint on wrapping.

Questions this page should answer:
What is at risk and what is not: discrete-log commitments, hash-based commitments, the ROM analysis in a quantum setting.
Hash-based signatures and aggregation, and why a SNARK is the aggregation mechanism. Which hash they are instantiated with is now SHA-2 or BLAKE rather than Poseidon.
Lattice-based commitments as an alternative, and their cost profile.
The consequence for the last step of a pipeline that currently ends in Groth16.
What VCV-io's lattice work already covers.
What bit-security a deployed system actually claims, under which assumptions, and who checked. This is where soundness regimes stop being a theoretical distinction.

Questions this page should answer:
The parameters real provers ship: rate, repetitions, grinding bits, field size — and the claimed level they add up to.
Which claims depend on a conjecture, and whether that is documented in the system's own materials.
The accounting across recursion layers, where errors compose.
Who is responsible for the number: protocol designers, implementers, or auditors.
What a machine-checked parameter calculation would look like, and whether it is a reasonable thing to build.

fr:title.text: A Note on Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Note on Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Hash Functions in Bitcoin and Ethereum is about what each chain actually hashes with, and about the Ethereum Foundation abandoning Poseidon for L1 on 13 August 2026. The reason is the interesting part: Poseidon did not break. Proof systems over binary fields made conventional hashes cheap enough to prove that decades of public cryptanalysis became the deciding factor instead.

The sections:
SHA-2 and the Bitcoin design — double SHA-256 for proof of work and transaction identifiers, RIPEMD-160 for legacy addresses, tagged hashes for Taproot.
Keccak and Ethereum — why keccak256 is not SHA-3, everywhere it names state, and the SHA-256 half of the protocol on the consensus layer.
The BLAKE family — 2s against 2b, what BLAKE3's tree mode buys, and which variant is actually a candidate.
Poseidon, and why Ethereum walked away — the HADES construction, the cryptanalysis initiative, and the Binius and Flock results that reversed the decision.

fr:title.text: A Corpus on zkVMs and SNARKs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A Corpus on zkVMs and SNARKs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: zkVMs and SNARKs is a new corpus on this site: a systematic study of the cryptography and machine architecture these systems are built from, one page per topic. It follows the pipeline every modern proof system follows, from a computation to a deployed proof, and it is the theory behind the snarkification work.

The sections:
The shape of a proof system — the definitions everything else is stated in, and where security is lost between an interactive protocol and a deployed one.
The algebraic and coding-theoretic toolkit — fields, polynomials, Reed–Solomon codes, proximity gaps, sumcheck.
Arithmetisation — R1CS, Plonkish, AIR, lookups, and Clean.
Polynomial commitment schemes, and low-degree testing from FRI through STIR to WHIR.
Proof systems in the wild and folding, recursion, and aggregation.
zkVMs — the stack, the systems in the field, and how they break.
Formalising the stack — ArkLib, CompPoly, and the rest of the verified-zkEVM effort.
The Ethereum setting, and a reading path through all of it.
I recently implemented a formally verified virtual machine in Lean on which you can run 2048 in terminal! Try it out!

The LC-3 is a small 16-bit instructional architecture: eight general-purpose registers, a program counter, condition flags, and a 2^{16}-word address space. At each step the machine fetches a word from memory at the PC, decodes it as one of fourteen opcodes (from arithmetic and bitwise operations to loads, stores, branches, jumps, and subroutine calls), then updates registers, memory, and control flow accordingly. Beyond those opcodes, LC-3 programs rely on trap routines for console I/O and on memory-mapped I/O for the keyboard—so a faithful simulator must implement both the core instructions and this I/O story. For more on the architecture, see here.

The code in LC3-Lean is laid out as follows:
register and flag state lives in LC3Lean/Registers.lean,
the flat memory model in LC3Lean/Memory.lean,
opcode decoding in LC3Lean/Instructions.lean,
the fetch–decode–execute step and per-opcode semantics in LC3Lean/Execution.lean,
The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean. If you open those modules, every informal claim in this paragraph—word size, register count, opcode coverage, traps, MMIO—is meant to be visible as definitions and executable code rather than hand-waving.
The runnable binary wires together loading of .obj files, the execution loop, and MMIO in Main.lean.
For full details, see this page.

"Formally verified" here means that Lean checks mathematical theorems relating the implementation above to an explicit ISA-level specification of how each instruction may read and write registers and memory. Those theorems are stated and proved in the LC3Correct package—especially LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean, with supporting lemmas about registers and memory in LC3Correct/RegisterLemmas.lean and LC3Correct/MemoryLemmas.lean. Together they aim to capture, opcode by opcode, that the Lean executor’s effect on machine state matches the spec encoded alongside it. All proofs pass without sorry!

The boundary worth keeping in mind is the thin C shim (c/terminal.c) used for POSIX terminal raw mode and polling: it affects how characters reach your screen and keyboard, but the LC-3 machine semantics and the correctness proofs live on the Lean side. Readers who want the precise logical statement for a single opcode should start from LC3Correct/ExecutionCorrect.lean and follow the definitions it references—the prose here is only a map to those lemmas.
For full details, see this page.
During Q1 of 2026 we worked building out CompPoly, a formally verified model of computable polynomials in Lean. The purpose of CompPoly is to provide a computable base for the specs in Arklib.

My thoughts on computable specifications are still developing. They are growing out of an interest during my PhD in the integrity of formal specifications in the case of smart contracts. zkVMs and SNARKS also have complicated specifications, but for a different reason than smart contracts. Whereas smart contract specifications have difficult-to-define, high-level, socio-economic properties that one must aim at with a spec, the specs of zkVMs are complex because they correspond to some pretty intense mathematics. Just stating the desired properties requires quite a bit of machinery -- see Arklib for a taste of that.

So, we can write complex mathematical specifications in Lean - great, what does computability add to this, or any specification? For one, it lets you run tests. Having tests lets you test the integrity of your spec and test it in sort of a meta- way. It helps build confidence that the spec was built out correctly, something that is difficult (impossible?) to really know.

I have written before about metaspecifications, or formal specifications of specifications, in the context of smart contracts. I really believe that metaspecifications can add a lot to the security of smart contracts, but a lot of theory has to be built up (even just developed from a cryptoeconomic point of view) before this becomes a reasonable strategy for contracts in the wild.

However, metaspecifications already show up in cryptography! An implementation has a specification, the design of the cryptographic system or protocol (e.g. FRI). The system or protocol is defined in mathematical terms, with assumptions, and with associated proofs of security. Security proofs (reduction proofs) show that if the cryptographic protocol fails, then some assumption of the system was violated. This is a metaspecification!

But, as with all specifications, it is very hard to be sure that your specification is correct. This is where computability comes in. Having an executable/computable specification means that you can run tests on it, further extending your specification in an informal way. It makes your spec act more like software, and in some sense makes it stronger as a specification because as a program that runs it is closer to the thing that you're verifying.

Lean is of course a great place for this. It is easy to go between computable and non-computable terms, spec and implementation, and more and more of the infrastructure of verification is becoming available in Lean.

There are ongoing efforts to "snarkify" Ethereum, i.e. to integrate zero knowledge proofs into every layer of the Ethereum protocol. I contribute to this via formal verification in Lean. My main focus is currently on CompPoly and Arklib.
See our website for more information.
